chunks: A pad that's solidly connected to a plane sits on a big heat sink: when I put a hot iron or a hot-air nozzle on it, the plane conducts the heat away as fast as I add it, so the joint struggles to reach solder liquidus, about 217 degrees for lead-free.
I end up overheating the area, lifting the pad, or giving up.
A thermal relief connects the pad through a few narrow spokes, so the pad behaves much more like an isolated pad and heats up quickly.

The catch is that power and ground components often need the low-resistance, low thermal resistance connection, so reliefs on those pads cost current capacity and heat spreading, and designers sometimes turn them off, for example on a power MOSFET's source or an exposed thermal pad.
Those joints are then the hardest to rework.

At the bench I'd compensate: preheat the board from underneath so the temperature step is smaller, use hot air or a big iron tip with lots of thermal mass, add fresh flux and sometimes a little leaded solder to lower the melting point, and take my time.
So reliefs are good for rework, solid connections are good for the circuit, and the layout has to pick per pad."
